nodes.title: Foundations and Core Language
nodes.description: This part groups chapters in this subject’s graduate book.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Fourier series
nodes.description: Fourier series decompose periodic functions into trigonometric modes. Different summation procedures produce different convergence behavior.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Orthogonal expansions
nodes.description: Fourier series decompose periodic functions into trigonometric modes. Orthogonality turns coefficients into coordinates in a Hilbert space.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Trigonometric systems
nodes.description: Trigonometric functions form an orthogonal system on the circle with the usual measure. Their span is dense in the corresponding L2 space.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Coefficients
nodes.description: Fourier coefficients are inner products with frequency modes. They measure how much of each oscillation is present.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Parseval identity
nodes.description: Parseval's identity equates the L2 norm with the squared sum of Fourier coefficients. It expresses conservation of energy between physical and frequency descriptions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Convergence and summability
nodes.description: Different summation procedures produce different convergence behavior. This section distinguishes norm convergence from pointwise reconstruction.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Pointwise and L2 convergence
nodes.description: L2 convergence follows from Hilbert-space completeness of the trigonometric system. Pointwise convergence requires separate hypotheses and arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Fejér kernels
nodes.description: Fejér kernels average Fourier partial sums using nonnegative kernels. They provide robust approximation for continuous periodic functions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Gibbs phenomenon
nodes.description: The Gibbs phenomenon is persistent overshoot near jumps in Fourier partial sums. It illustrates why pointwise convergence does not imply uniform accuracy.

nodes.title: Fourier transform on the line

nodes.title: Schwartz class
nodes.description: The Schwartz class consists of smooth functions with rapid decay of every derivative. It is an especially stable setting for Fourier transformation.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Test functions
nodes.description: Schwartz functions provide a test space for tempered distributions. Their regularity and decay justify many initial calculations.

nodes.title: Decay
nodes.description: Rapid decay controls functions and derivatives after multiplication by arbitrary polynomial weights. It makes Fourier integrals and differentiation arguments well behaved.

nodes.title: Inversion formula

nodes.title: L2 theory

nodes.title: Plancherel theorem
nodes.description: Plancherel's theorem preserves the L2 inner product under Fourier transformation. It creates a frequency representation for square-integrable functions.

nodes.title: Extension by density
nodes.description: A bounded map on a dense subspace extends uniquely to the completion. This constructs the L2 transform from Schwartz functions.

nodes.title: Uncertainty principles
nodes.description: Uncertainty principles prevent simultaneous concentration in position and frequency. They quantify the tradeoff inherent in localization.

nodes.title: Convolution and approximation
nodes.description: Convolution averages one function against translated copies of another. Special kernels realize smoothing and boundary-extension processes.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Convolution algebra
nodes.description: Convolution averages one function against translated copies of another. Its algebra is central to smoothing and translation-invariant operators.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Fubini
nodes.description: Fubini justifies exchanging the integrals occurring in convolution identities. The required absolute-integrability conditions must be checked.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Young inequality
nodes.description: Young's inequality bounds a convolution in an Lp space using norms of its factors. The exponent relation determines the admissible mapping property.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Approximate identities
nodes.description: Approximate identities concentrate mass near the origin with controlled total size. Their convolutions recover functions in suitable convergence modes.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Summability kernels
nodes.description: Special kernels realize smoothing and boundary-extension processes. Their limiting behavior connects analysis of operators with approximation.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Approximation to identity
nodes.description: Approximation to the identity uses kernels converging toward point concentration. Density and translation continuity establish convergence of their convolutions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Poisson kernel
nodes.description: The Poisson kernel produces harmonic extensions and boundary approximations. It links Fourier multipliers with potential theory.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Heat kernel
nodes.description: The heat kernel solves the heat equation by convolution. Its Gaussian scaling explains diffusion and smoothing.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Lp estimates and interpolation
nodes.description: Interpolation obtains intermediate bounds from endpoint information. Endpoint estimates frequently fail in ordinary strong Lp norms.

nodes.title: Interpolation principles
nodes.description: Interpolation obtains intermediate bounds from endpoint information. It reduces the number of operator estimates that need direct proof.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Convexity of operator bounds
nodes.description: Operator bounds often vary logarithmically convexly with reciprocal exponents. This geometry guides interpolation between known estimates.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Riesz–Thorin theorem
nodes.description: Riesz–Thorin interpolates strong bounds for linear operators between Lp spaces. Its complex-analytic proof uses analytic families and the three-lines principle.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Marcinkiewicz theorem
nodes.description: Marcinkiewicz interpolation converts suitable weak endpoint bounds into strong interior bounds for sublinear operators. It is essential for maximal and singular-integral estimates.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Endpoint behavior
nodes.description: Endpoint estimates frequently fail in ordinary strong Lp norms. Distribution functions and refined spaces capture the remaining control.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Weak-type estimates
nodes.description: A weak-type bound controls the measure of superlevel sets of an operator output. It can hold even when the corresponding strong norm estimate fails.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Distribution functions
nodes.description: A distribution function records the measure of points where a function exceeds a given magnitude. Layer-cake formulas connect it to integral norms.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Lorentz-space motivation
nodes.description: Lorentz spaces refine Lp spaces using rearrangements and distribution functions. They describe endpoint behavior more precisely.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Maximal functions and differentiation
nodes.description: Covering arguments select controlled subfamilies of balls from complicated collections. Maximal inequalities control exceptional sets in local averaging limits.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Covering lemmas
nodes.description: Covering arguments select controlled subfamilies of balls from complicated collections. They convert local averaging information into global measure bounds.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Vitali and Besicovitch ideas
nodes.description: Vitali and Besicovitch covering principles organize overlaps among balls. Their geometric conclusions drive differentiation and maximal estimates.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Maximal operator
nodes.description: The Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator takes the supremum of local absolute averages. It detects where a function has unusually large local mass.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Weak (1,1) estimate
nodes.description: The weak (1,1) estimate bounds maximal-function superlevel measure by the L1 norm divided by the threshold. A covering lemma supplies the main argument.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Differentiation consequences
nodes.description: Maximal inequalities control exceptional sets in local averaging limits. This produces differentiation and density conclusions almost everywhere.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Lebesgue differentiation
nodes.description: Lebesgue differentiation recovers an integrable function from shrinking averages almost everywhere. Maximal estimates control the error after approximation by continuous functions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Density points
nodes.description: A density point is a point where a measurable set occupies asymptotically all of small neighborhoods. Almost every point of a measurable set has this property.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Maximal inequalities
nodes.description: Maximal inequalities bound the size of exceptional sets uniformly over averaging scales. They are a standard route from dense subclasses to general functions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Singular integrals
nodes.description: Singular kernels require cancellation because their absolute size may not be integrable near the diagonal. Calderón–Zygmund theory combines kernel regularity with boundedness and decomposition arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Kernel conditions
nodes.description: Singular kernels require cancellation because their absolute size may not be integrable near the diagonal. Truncations define manageable approximations to the operator.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Size and cancellation
nodes.description: Kernel size bounds control singular growth, while cancellation offsets that growth. Both are needed in standard singular-integral theories.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Principal values
nodes.description: A principal value is a limit with a prescribed symmetric exclusion of the singularity. Existence must be proved rather than assumed.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Truncations
nodes.description: Truncated operators remove a neighborhood of the singularity. Uniform estimates allow a limit operator to be defined and controlled.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Calderón–Zygmund theory
nodes.description: Calderón–Zygmund theory combines kernel regularity with boundedness and decomposition arguments. It extends singular-integral estimates across a range of exponents.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: L2 estimates
nodes.description: L2 estimates give an initial boundedness result, often through Fourier methods. They serve as an anchor for wider Lp theory.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Decomposition
nodes.description: The Calderón–Zygmund decomposition splits a function into controlled good and localized bad parts. Cancellation of the bad parts compensates for their large size.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Lp boundedness
nodes.description: Lp boundedness follows from endpoint estimates and interpolation under the theorem's kernel assumptions. The permissible exponent range is part of the result.

nodes.title: Littlewood–Paley methods
nodes.description: Dyadic frequency decomposition separates a function into scales. Littlewood–Paley estimates characterize function norms through frequency pieces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Frequency decompositions
nodes.description: Dyadic frequency decomposition separates a function into scales. It makes regularity and interaction between frequencies visible.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Dyadic partitions
nodes.description: A dyadic partition divides frequency space into regions of geometrically increasing size. Smooth cutoffs keep the associated operators manageable.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Projections
nodes.description: Frequency projections extract the pieces selected by a partition. Their almost-orthogonality supports reconstruction and norm estimates.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Square functions
nodes.description: A square function aggregates the magnitudes of pieces quadratically. It measures the collective contribution of different scales.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Function-space estimates
nodes.description: Littlewood–Paley estimates characterize function norms through frequency pieces. They provide tools for regularity and nonlinear product estimates.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Square-function inequalities
nodes.description: Square-function inequalities compare a function's norm with the norm of its scale aggregate. They extend orthogonality ideas beyond L2.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Sobolev characterization
nodes.description: Sobolev regularity can be expressed through weighted frequency-piece norms. This translates differentiability into quantitative scale decay.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Paraproduct motivation
nodes.description: Paraproducts separate products into low-high and comparable-frequency interactions. They organize nonlinear estimates that ordinary multiplication obscures.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Oscillatory and restriction estimates
nodes.description: Oscillatory integrals gain decay through cancellation in rapidly varying phases. Fourier restriction asks when a Fourier transform has a meaningful trace on a curved set.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Oscillatory integrals
nodes.description: Oscillatory integrals gain decay through cancellation in rapidly varying phases. The geometry of stationary points determines the estimate.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Van der Corput lemma
nodes.description: Van der Corput estimates use lower bounds on suitable phase derivatives. They provide elementary control of one-dimensional oscillatory integrals.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Stationary phase
nodes.description: Stationary phase approximates integrals near nondegenerate critical points of the phase. It identifies leading asymptotic contributions and decay rates.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Decay estimates
nodes.description: Decay estimates quantify cancellation as an oscillation parameter grows. Their rate depends on phase geometry and amplitude regularity.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Restriction phenomena
nodes.description: Fourier restriction asks when a Fourier transform has a meaningful trace on a curved set. Curvature and integrability determine what bounds can hold.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Fourier restriction problem
nodes.description: The restriction problem seeks estimates for transforms restricted to lower-dimensional surfaces. Such traces are not defined for arbitrary Lp transforms without additional control.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Maximal estimates
nodes.description: Maximal estimates control a supremum over a family of Fourier-related operators. They often support almost-everywhere convergence and restriction applications.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Selected applications
nodes.description: Restriction estimates feed dispersive PDE bounds and geometric measure problems. Each application must match dimensions, exponents, and curvature hypotheses.

nodes.title: Harmonic analysis on groups
nodes.description: Compact groups generalize periodic domains as spaces for harmonic decomposition. Locally compact groups support convolution and representations through Haar integration.

nodes.title: Compact groups
nodes.description: Compact groups generalize periodic domains as spaces for harmonic decomposition. Haar measure and representation theory replace ordinary trigonometric coordinates.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Haar measure
nodes.description: Haar measure is translation invariant and can be normalized to total mass one on a compact group. It defines the integrals used in group Fourier analysis.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Characters
nodes.description: Characters are traces of representations and encode conjugacy-invariant information. For compact abelian groups, one-dimensional characters play the role of Fourier modes.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Peter–Weyl theorem
nodes.description: Peter–Weyl gives density and orthogonality properties of finite-dimensional unitary matrix coefficients. It generalizes Fourier expansion on compact groups.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Locally compact groups
nodes.description: Locally compact groups support convolution and representations through Haar integration. The abelian case admits a particularly direct duality theory.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Convolution and representations
nodes.description: Convolution combines group functions using multiplication and Haar measure. Representations turn these convolutions into operator products.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Abelian duality
nodes.description: Pontryagin duality relates a locally compact abelian group to its character group. It extends Fourier analysis beyond Euclidean and periodic settings.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Examples
nodes.description: The line, the circle, discrete groups, and finite groups provide complementary examples. Comparing them reveals the common transform architecture.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Applications and advanced directions
nodes.description: Harmonic estimates translate differential operators into frequency-space problems. Further topics refine localization in scale, position, and frequency.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: PDE applications
nodes.description: Harmonic estimates translate differential operators into frequency-space problems. This gives tools for propagation and regularity in PDE.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Dispersive estimates
nodes.description: Dispersive estimates quantify spreading and decay of oscillatory evolution. They are building blocks for space-time estimates of solutions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Elliptic regularity
nodes.description: Elliptic regularity controls derivatives through elliptic equations and their data. Fourier methods provide transparent proofs in constant-coefficient model cases.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Multiplier methods
nodes.description: Multiplier methods study operators that multiply Fourier transforms by a symbol. Symbol conditions determine their mapping properties on function spaces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Further topics
nodes.description: Further topics refine localization in scale, position, and frequency. They connect the core theory to data representations and difficult geometric questions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Wavelets
nodes.description: Wavelets use translated and dilated building blocks to represent functions. They combine scale information with spatial localization.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Time-frequency analysis
nodes.description: Time-frequency analysis studies simultaneous localization in both variables. It is useful when a single global frequency decomposition is too coarse.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.description: Analytic number theory and fractal restriction use oscillation under arithmetic or geometric constraints. These routes require specialized estimates beyond the core course.
